You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 29 year old man 3 months after commencing olanzapine 15 mg orally each evening for a first episode of schizophrenia. He has stopped hearing voices and is looking for work. His weight has risen from 82 kg to 90 kg over the 3 months, his waist circumference is 102 cm, and he smokes 10 cigarettes daily. He has no personal or family history of diabetes and does not drink alcohol.

Baseline fasting glucose was 4.9 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4) and fasting lipids were within normal limits. Blood pressure today is 132/84 mmHg. He asks how often he now needs blood tests since he is feeling well and has commenced full-time TAFE study.

data_table.Weight trajectory: 82 kg baseline to 90 kg at 3 months; waist circumference 102 cm
data_table.Baseline metabolics: Fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); fasting lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose and lipids now, then every 3 months for the first year on treatment
options.rationale: RANZCP and eTG recommend fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks after starting a second-generation antipsychotic then quarterly during the first year, with weight and waist at every visit; olanzapine carries the highest metabolic burden and this patient's early weight gain and central adiposity make quarterly checks appropriate (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

options.text: Defer any fasting bloods until 12 months after commencement then repeat glucose and lipids
options.rationale: Waiting a full year misses the first-year risk window when metabolic derangement on olanzapine is most likely to emerge and be reversible with early switch or lifestyle input (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

options.text: Order an oral glucose tolerance test today and only recheck fasting bloods if the OGTT is impaired
options.rationale: OGTT is reserved for equivocal fasting glucose or high-risk patients with normal fasting values; the routine surveillance test is fasting glucose plus HbA1c, not baseline OGTT for every antipsychotic patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Rely on annual GP well person checks for metabolic surveillance while he remains on olanzapine
options.rationale: Annual only monitoring is inadequate for a high-metabolic-risk antipsychotic in the first year; delegating without a shared plan misses the point of shared care and lets weight and glycaemia drift (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

options.text: Measure only weight and blood pressure quarterly and skip fasting bloods while glucose remains normal
options.rationale: Weight and blood pressure alone underdetect dyslipidaemia and dysglycaemia on olanzapine; the first-year plan includes fasting glucose or HbA1c plus lipids at 12 weeks and quarterly thereafter (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, particularly olanzapine and clozapine, produce most of their metabolic harm in the first year. RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic set 12 week fasting bloods with quarterly repeat through year one, alongside weight and waist at every review. Early weight gain of 8 kg with a rising waist justifies rather than deferring the recommended schedule. Only after the first year does the interval extend to 6 to 12 months if metrics are stable. Skipping fasting glucose in favour of weight alone underdetects the dysglycaemia this drug class produces.
key_points: 12 week fasting glucose and lipids after starting a second-generation antipsychotic
Repeat quarterly during the first year, then 6 to 12 monthly if stable
Weight and waist every visit; blood pressure at each review
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine causes the largest early weight and lipid shift in its class; a rising waist at 12 weeks predicts future dysglycaemia and should trigger active lifestyle input, not a passive wait.

stem:
You are the on-call psychiatry registrar in a tertiary emergency department. A 41 year old woman with known bipolar I disorder, previously on lithium 750 mg orally each evening, was brought in by her partner because she has stopped speaking, sat rigidly in the shower for 4 hours, and did not respond when he attempted to move her. On examination she is mute, holds her right arm in whichever position you place it, resists your passive movements of her left arm, and stares without blinking through your assessment.

Her partner reports her lithium was ceased 2 weeks ago after a routine level of 1.4 mmol/L (0.4 to 1.0), and she has been sleeping less than 3 hours nightly and pacing the hall. Vital signs are pulse 96, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C. Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, TSH, creatine kinase, and non contrast CT head are within normal limits.

data_table.Motor findings: Mute; posturing right arm; gegenhalten left arm; staring without blinking
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, temp 37.1
data_table.Recent medication change: Lithium stopped 2 weeks ago (level then 1.4 mmol/L)
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TSH, CK, CT head within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg for acute behavioural disturbance now
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and raise the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome; catatonia should be treated with benzodiazepines or ECT before any antipsychotic reintroduction (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance).

options.text: Arrange an urgent electroencephalogram to exclude non convulsive status epilepticus before any treatment
options.rationale: Non convulsive status is a differential, but a lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic and does not delay EEG if the response is inadequate; EEG first is not the immediate step in a classic catatonia presentation (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance).

options.text: Give lorazepam 2 mg intravenously as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and reassess within 15 minutes
options.rationale: A parenteral lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM, repeated after 15 minutes if no response) is the recommended first step for suspected catatonia; a partial response confirms the syndrome and predicts benefit from scheduled benzodiazepine therapy (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance).

options.text: Recommence lithium at the previous dose and monitor level in 48 hours before any other intervention
options.rationale: Restarting lithium is appropriate mood stabilisation over days but does not address acute catatonia, which needs benzodiazepine or ECT within hours to prevent physical complications (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance).

options.text: Arrange same day electroconvulsive therapy without a benzodiazepine trial as first line management
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective and first line for malignant or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia, but a lorazepam challenge is the initial step; ECT follows if the challenge fails or the patient becomes autonomically unstable (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance).

explanation.summary: Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, and staring in a patient with a known mood disorder is catatonia until proven otherwise, and a parenteral lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic. RANZCP guidance recommends 1 to 2 mg IV or IM lorazepam with reassessment within 15 minutes; a partial response supports scheduled benzodiazepine dosing (up to 8 to 24 mg daily in divided doses). Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and are avoided until the syndrome resolves. ECT is reserved for refractory or malignant cases and for autonomic instability. Lithium reintroduction addresses the underlying bipolar illness but is not the acute step.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM is the diagnostic challenge
Reassess within 15 minutes; repeat if no response
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves to limit NMS risk
explanation.pearls: A positive lorazepam challenge (partial resolution of mutism or posturing within 15 minutes) predicts benefit from scheduled benzodiazepines at 8 mg daily or more; failure at 4 mg total should prompt ECT planning.

You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with 2 days of right flank pain, rigors, and vomiting. She reports urinary frequency and dysuria since yesterday. She has no medical history, no known allergies, is not pregnant (urine bhCG negative), and takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill.

On examination she is flushed with right costovertebral angle tenderness. Pulse 108, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Urinalysis shows leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 2+. Urine and blood cultures are collected. Full blood count shows white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45 to 90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). She is able to tolerate oral fluids after antiemetic but still has rigors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98% RA, temp 38.9
data_table.Bloods: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L; creatinine 82 micromol/L; lactate 1.8 mmol/L
data_table.Cultures: Urine and blood cultures collected before antibiotics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen at this point?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for 10 days with early GP review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral cefalexin is not recommended for empirical pyelonephritis because of poor tissue penetration and unreliable coverage of resistant Enterobacterales (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 14 days without empirical intravenous cover
options.rationale: Trimethoprim resistance in Australian E coli approaches 25 percent and it is not adequate empirical therapy for pyelonephritis; a beta lactam or aminoglycoside is preferred while cultures are awaited (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral fluconazole 200 mg for empirical yeast cover
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone dosing for pyelonephritis is correct, but empirical antifungal is not indicated without evidence of candiduria in a catheterised or immunocompromised patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg per kg with amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours pending culture results
options.rationale: Gentamicin plus amoxicillin is the eTG first-line empirical regimen for hospitalised pyelonephritis in a non pregnant adult without penicillin allergy; the combination covers Enterobacterales and enterococci and can be narrowed once cultures return (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours for broad spectrum cover pending culture results
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for confirmed or high risk multidrug resistant infection or severe sepsis in a colonised patient; first line empirical use undermines antimicrobial stewardship (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Australian empirical therapy for hospitalised acute pyelonephritis in a non pregnant adult with no penicillin allergy is intravenous gentamicin 5 mg per kg once daily plus amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours, or ceftriaxone 1 g once daily as monotherapy where an aminoglycoside is contraindicated. Cultures are collected before the first dose, and switch to oral therapy occurs after 24 to 48 hours of clinical improvement, tailored to susceptibility. Trimethoprim, cefalexin, and empirical antifungals are inappropriate for hospitalised pyelonephritis. Carbapenems are reserved for confirmed multidrug resistance or severe sepsis with concerning colonisation.
key_points: First line: gentamicin plus amoxicillin IV, or ceftriaxone IV alone
Cultures before first dose; tailor once susceptibilities available
Total 10 to 14 days including step down to oral therapy
explanation.pearls: Once daily gentamicin at 5 mg per kg gives high peak concentration for gram negative killing and is safer than divided dosing; check level before the second dose.

You are the GP registrar reviewing a 46 year old man with schizoaffective disorder stabilised on aripiprazole 15 mg daily for 3 years. He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily since age 18, has made two prior quit attempts with nicotine gum alone that lasted 3 weeks each. He has no history of seizures, no cardiovascular disease, and no depressive symptoms today (PHQ-9 score 4). He drinks 2 standard drinks weekly and works as a warehouse supervisor.

He describes strong urges within 5 minutes of waking and after meals, and would like a medication that works better than gum. He has heard varenicline is more effective but is worried about mood effects because of his mental health history. Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, weight 88 kg, spirometry FEV1 78 percent predicted.

data_table.Smoking pattern: 25 cigarettes daily since age 18; first within 5 minutes of waking
data_table.Prior attempts: Two 3 week quit attempts on nicotine gum monotherapy
data_table.Mental health: Schizoaffective disorder stable on aripiprazole; PHQ-9 4

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy for this quit attempt?

options.text: Continue nicotine gum monotherapy as needed with a target quit date in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Monotherapy nicotine gum has already failed twice; escalation to a combination NRT or non nicotine agent is expected before another single agent attempt (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guide).

options.text: Prescribe bupropion 150 mg orally daily titrated to 150 mg twice daily and set a quit date at 2 weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but is contraindicated with seizure risk factors and its psychiatric interaction profile with antipsychotics is less favourable than varenicline in schizoaffective disorder (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guide).

options.text: Recommend electronic cigarette prescription only pathway as a harm minimisation strategy for 3 months
options.rationale: The TGA prescription only nicotine vaping product pathway is a second line consideration for patients who have failed first line pharmacotherapy, not a first line agent (Source: TGA Nicotine Vaping Product Guidance).

options.text: Prescribe nortriptyline 25 mg daily titrating to 75 mg nightly across 4 weeks as smoking cessation aid
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a fourth line option with anticholinergic burden and QT risk; it is not preferred in a patient on a QT prolonging antipsychotic (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guide).

options.text: Prescribe varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated to 1 mg twice daily with a quit date at 8 to 14 days
options.rationale: The RACGP guide places varenicline as most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation; the EAGLES trial showed no increase in neuropsychiatric events in stable mental illness, and titration with a quit date at day 8 to 14 is the standard schedule (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guide).

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation in adults and is safe in stable mental illness based on the EAGLES trial. The RACGP schedule starts at 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily, with a quit date set between days 8 and 14. Bupropion is contraindicated with seizure risk factors and has less favourable psychiatric profile than varenicline. Vaping is a second line pathway. Monotherapy NRT can suffice for lighter smokers, but a heavy smoker with two failed NRT attempts merits escalation.
key_points: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated to 1 mg twice daily
Quit date set at day 8 to 14, then continue 12 weeks
EAGLES trial supports use in stable schizophrenia and mood disorders
explanation.pearls: Warn about vivid dreams and nausea (both common in first fortnight); mood or suicidal ideation warrants prompt review but is not more common than placebo in EAGLES.

stem:
You are the on-call medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium carbonate 900 mg orally each evening for 24 years. She was brought in by her daughter with 3 days of nausea, coarse tremor, unsteady gait, and today intermittent confusion. She takes no other prescribed medications; her GP added ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily 10 days ago for shoulder pain, and she has been drinking cranberry juice for what she thought was cystitis over the last week. Her last lithium level 8 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (0.4 to 1.0), and her last creatinine 6 months ago was 78 micromol/L (45 to 90).

On presentation she is drowsy but rousable, has a coarse rest tremor, and truncal ataxia. Vital signs are pulse 82, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8. Bloods now show lithium 2.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90). ECG shows sinus rhythm with T wave flattening.

data_table.Recent medication change: Ibuprofen 400 mg tds started 10 days ago
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 148/92, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8
data_table.Prior baseline: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L 8 months ago; creatinine 78 micromol/L 6 months ago

lead_in: Which factor is the single most likely primary precipitant of this toxicity?

options.text: Age related decline in glomerular filtration rate in a lithium naive patient at baseline
options.rationale: Age related eGFR decline is gradual and does not typically produce an acute doubling of creatinine over days; a specific precipitant is required to explain the acute rise (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drug reduction of renal lithium clearance from prostaglandin blockade
options.rationale: NSAIDs reduce afferent arteriolar prostaglandin dependent vasodilation, cutting GFR and lithium clearance; the temporal association with ibuprofen initiation 10 days ago and creatinine doubling identifies this as the primary precipitant (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Cranberry juice mediated induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 lithium metabolism
options.rationale: Lithium undergoes essentially no hepatic metabolism and is cleared unchanged by the kidneys; cranberry juice is not the mechanism here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Loss of sodium through mild diarrhoea leading to lithium redistribution from erythrocytes to plasma
options.rationale: Volume depletion and low salt intake raise lithium levels through proximal tubular sodium and lithium reabsorption, but there is no reported gastrointestinal loss in this scenario; the mechanism described is inaccurate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cumulative interstitial nephritis from decades of lithium therapy causing tubular resistance to elimination
options.rationale: Chronic lithium nephropathy is a slow decline over decades and does not explain an acute doubling of creatinine and a lithium level rise over 10 days; it is a background risk, not the acute precipitant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Any drug that reduces renal perfusion or afferent arteriolar prostaglandin activity raises lithium concentration acutely. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and thiazide diuretics are the classical precipitants. Here ibuprofen at 400 mg three times daily started 10 days ago aligns with a doubling of creatinine and a lithium level of 2.4 mmol/L in a previously stable patient. Management is cessation of the offending agent, intravenous saline (avoiding hypotonic fluids), continuous cardiac monitoring, and haemodialysis when the level exceeds 4 mmol/L, when neurotoxicity persists, or renal function is severely impaired.
key_points: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides raise lithium acutely
Confusion plus level above 2.0 mmol/L is severe toxicity
Dialysis threshold: level above 4 mmol/L or refractory neurotoxicity
explanation.pearls: A level of 2.5 mmol/L with normal renal function may be managed with saline alone; the same level with rising creatinine or refractory neurology needs urgent renal replacement therapy.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnostic criteria and functional impairment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar assessing a 27 year old graphic designer who describes lifelong difficulty finishing projects, chronic lateness, and losing wallets and keys weekly. She was described in Year 4 school reports as bright but not applying herself. She has been terminated from two jobs in the last 3 years for missed deadlines and now spends most weekend evenings catching up on work she was unable to complete on weekdays. She has never taken stimulant medication.

She scored 5 on the PHQ-9, 4 on the GAD-7, and 22 on the Adult ADHD Self Report Scale part A. Her collateral history from her mother confirms restlessness and inattention in primary school despite average academic ability. She uses no alcohol, cannabis, or stimulants. Thyroid function, ferritin, and full blood count are within normal limits. She asks whether she meets criteria for adult ADHD.

data_table.Onset history: Restlessness and inattention documented from Year 4 reports and by mother
data_table.Functional impairment: Two employment terminations in 3 years; weekend catch up work

lead_in: Which criterion is the most decisive in confirming DSM-5 adult ADHD in this presentation?

options.text: Symptoms present in more than one setting with clear functional impairment and childhood onset
options.rationale: DSM-5 adult ADHD requires several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12, in two or more settings, with clear evidence of impairment; this scenario meets all three (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: A positive Adult ADHD Self Report Scale total score above 20 with contemporaneous PHQ-9 below 10
options.rationale: ASRS is a screening tool and mood exclusion does not by itself confirm ADHD; the DSM-5 diagnosis rests on symptoms, cross-situational impairment, and childhood onset (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: A positive short trial response to methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily over 2 weeks
options.rationale: Stimulant responsiveness is not diagnostic; healthy adults also experience cognitive enhancement, and empirical trials are not used to confirm the disorder (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

options.text: An informant confirmed history of restlessness during adolescence rather than primary school onset
options.rationale: DSM-5 requires onset of several symptoms before age 12, not before adolescence; an adolescent onset alone excludes the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Neuropsychological testing showing global working memory in the low average range on formal measures
options.rationale: Neuropsychological test scores do not confirm or exclude adult ADHD; the disorder is a clinical diagnosis and cognitive testing is complementary rather than definitive (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD in DSM-5 requires five or more inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (rather than six for children), several present before age 12, symptoms in two or more settings, and clear evidence of interference with functioning. Symptoms must not be better explained by another mental disorder or substance effect. This patient has school reports, maternal collateral, cross-setting symptoms (work and home), and unambiguous functional loss. ASRS is a screen, not a diagnosis. Stimulant challenges are not diagnostic and neuropsychology is supportive rather than definitive.
key_points: DSM-5 requires several symptoms before age 12
Symptoms in two or more settings with functional impairment
Screening tools (ASRS) support but do not confirm the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about primary school reports and third party history; adults commonly reconstruct their childhood as unremarkable, but school reports and parental recall carry more diagnostic weight than adult recall alone.

stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar seeing a 32 year old man who took an unknown quantity of amitriptyline 3 hours ago after a relationship breakdown. He is drowsy but rousable, has warm dry skin, and dilated pupils. On arrival his pulse is 132, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.4. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L. Serum paracetamol is not detected.

A 12 lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 132 with QRS duration 118 ms and a prominent terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. He becomes more difficult to rouse over the next 5 minutes. Intravenous access is established and cardiac monitoring is in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 92/58, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, temp 37.4
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia; QRS 118 ms; R wave aVR 4 mm
data_table.Toxicology: Paracetamol not detected; amitriptyline overdose 3 hours ago

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate management step?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse tricyclic mediated central nervous system depression
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not tricyclics, and may precipitate seizures in the context of co-ingestion or established TCA toxicity (Source: eviQ Poisons Information / Toxicology Guidance).

options.text: Give intravenous phenytoin 15 mg per kg over 30 minutes as prophylaxis against seizures and arrhythmia
options.rationale: Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker in its own right and worsens tricyclic mediated conduction slowing; it is contraindicated in TCA toxicity (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu).
source_refs: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu

options.text: Perform gastric lavage now to remove residual amitriptyline from the stomach 3 hours post-ingestion
options.rationale: Gastric lavage is not recommended more than 1 to 2 hours after ingestion of most agents and its use in TCA overdose has never shown mortality benefit (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu).
source_refs: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion titrated to mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg via central access
options.rationale: Pressors have a role but only after correction of acidosis and sodium channel blockade; jumping to noradrenaline without sodium bicarbonate misses the primary toxicological intervention (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu).
source_refs: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol as a bolus and repeat guided by QRS narrowing and pH
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms with R wave in aVR above 3 mm predicts arrhythmia and seizures in tricyclic toxicity; sodium bicarbonate boluses (1 to 2 mmol per kg) target QRS narrowing and blood pH of 7.45 to 7.55 by overcoming sodium channel blockade and alkalinising the plasma (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu).
source_refs: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu

explanation.summary: Tricyclic overdose kills through sodium channel blockade producing wide complex arrhythmia and seizures. QRS duration above 100 ms and an R wave in aVR above 3 mm both predict serious complications. Immediate management is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol per kg boluses aiming to narrow QRS and lift plasma pH to 7.45 to 7.55, followed by intubation for airway protection, benzodiazepines for seizure prophylaxis, and vasopressors only after sodium loading has been optimised. Phenytoin, flumazenil, and gastric lavage are contraindicated or unhelpful. Intralipid is second line for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate and pressors.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms or R wave in aVR above 3 mm predict arrhythmia
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol per kg boluses target pH 7.45 to 7.55
Avoid phenytoin, class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics, and flumazenil
explanation.pearls: In TCA cardiac arrest, hyperventilation and continuous sodium bicarbonate infusion form the mainstay; intralipid 20 percent 1.5 mL per kg bolus is reserved for arrest refractory to standard resuscitation and bicarbonate.

sources.label: Australian Toxicology Handbook - Murray, Little, Pascu

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder first line treatment
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar seeing a 24 year old woman on the second visit after her third emergency department presentation this year with self cutting. Her forearms show 20 or more parallel superficial cuts of varying age. She describes 5 years of unstable relationships, intense fear of abandonment, chronic emptiness, dissociative episodes lasting hours after arguments, and impulsive spending. She meets 7 of the 9 DSM-5 borderline personality disorder criteria.

Her mood is reactive rather than sustained: PHQ-9 12, GAD-7 14. She has no manic history and no psychotic symptoms. She uses alcohol only socially, no illicit substances. She has been prescribed quetiapine 100 mg nightly by her GP and sertraline 50 mg daily by a previous psychiatrist; she reports neither helped. She asks what treatment is actually going to help.

data_table.Presentations this year: Three ED attendances with self cutting
data_table.Current medications: Quetiapine 100 mg nocte; sertraline 50 mg daily (both unhelpful)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate primary treatment recommendation?

options.text: Add low dose olanzapine 5 mg nightly for mood instability and emptiness while continuing sertraline
options.rationale: NHMRC guidance and Cochrane reviews find no medication with meaningful benefit for the core features of borderline personality disorder; polypharmacy adds harm without benefit (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Refer for structured, time limited psychotherapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation based therapy
options.rationale: The NHMRC guideline recommends a structured, evidence based psychotherapy delivered by trained clinicians as the primary treatment for borderline personality disorder; DBT, MBT, transference focused psychotherapy, and schema therapy have the strongest evidence (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Admit to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit for a planned 4 to 6 week stabilisation and behavioural monitoring
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient admission for uncomplicated borderline personality disorder can reinforce dependence and self harm without changing long term outcome; brief admission is reserved for imminent risk (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily and reassess for reduction in cutting frequency in 6 weeks
options.rationale: SSRIs have very limited effect on borderline personality disorder core features and do not reliably reduce self harm; escalation without a psychological plan is not recommended (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Refer to a private hypnotherapist for weekly regression work on early attachment relationships
options.rationale: Hypnotic regression is not an evidence based treatment for borderline personality disorder and is not recommended by the NHMRC guideline (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

explanation.summary: The 2013 NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder places structured evidence based psychotherapy at the centre of treatment. Dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy, transference focused psychotherapy, and schema therapy have the most consistent evidence for reducing self harm, emergency presentations, and improving function. Medication has no demonstrated benefit for the core features and should be used only for defined co-occurring conditions and time limited crisis management. Brief admission is reserved for imminent risk; prolonged admission can be iatrogenic. Care coordination, a written safety plan, and consistent multidisciplinary follow up are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, TFP, schema) is the primary treatment
Medications have no evidence for core BPD features
Brief admission only for imminent risk
explanation.pearls: A written safety plan (early warning signs, coping strategies, contact numbers, means restriction) reduces subsequent self harm and is standard of care after any BPD presentation.

stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with 45 minutes of interscapular pain that woke him from sleep. He describes it as tearing, radiating to the left flank, and he vomited once at home. He has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 30 years, and quit 4 years ago. His father died aged 62 of a ruptured aorta.

He is diaphoretic. Vital signs are pulse 96 regular, blood pressure 176/104 mmHg right arm and 138/82 mmHg left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.9. Chest auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His left radial pulse is diminished compared with the right. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria; no ST elevation. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Bedside troponin is not elevated. High-sensitivity D-dimer is 4.2 mg/L (less than 0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP right arm 176/104, BP left arm 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, temp 36.9
data_table.Bedside findings: Diaphoretic; diminished left radial pulse; early diastolic murmur LSE
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm; LVH by voltage; no ST elevation
data_table.Investigations: Widened mediastinum on CXR; troponin negative; D-dimer 4.2 mg/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trans thoracic echocardiogram at the bedside to look for aortic root dilatation and regurgitation
options.rationale: TTE has limited sensitivity for type A or B dissection (about 60 percent) and cannot delineate the extent needed for surgical planning; CT angiography is the primary diagnostic in a stable patient (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Repeat high-sensitivity troponin at 1 hour and reassess for type 2 myocardial infarction cause
options.rationale: Serial troponin has utility for ACS assessment but does not evaluate the primary concern of dissection when clinical features and imaging are highly suggestive; further delay risks rupture (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Coronary angiography via right radial access to exclude an unstable ostial coronary lesion
options.rationale: Coronary angiography in an undiagnosed dissection risks catheter entry of the false lumen and delays definitive management; ACS is not the leading differential given asymmetric arm pressures and widened mediastinum (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Contrast enhanced computed tomography angiography of the aorta from arch to iliac bifurcation now
options.rationale: CT angiography of the whole aorta is the primary diagnostic in a haemodynamically stable patient with suspected acute aortic dissection; it delineates entry tear, extent, branch vessel involvement, and guides surgical or endovascular decisions (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Magnetic resonance angiography of the aorta with gadolinium contrast within the next 24 hours
options.rationale: MR angiography has excellent characterisation but scanner availability and scan duration make it impractical for the initial evaluation of suspected acute dissection; it is reserved for follow up or contrast allergic patients (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

explanation.summary: Tearing interscapular pain, asymmetric arm blood pressures (a difference above 20 mmHg), aortic regurgitation, diminished peripheral pulse, and a widened mediastinum in a hypertensive smoker with family history of aortic disease form a high probability presentation of acute aortic dissection. The primary diagnostic in a haemodynamically stable patient is CT angiography of the entire aorta (arch to iliac) to define classification (Stanford A vs B), branch vessel involvement, and surgical or endovascular strategy. Concurrently, target heart rate below 60 with intravenous esmolol or labetalol before adding a vasodilator, and involve cardiothoracic surgery for type A. Serial troponin, TTE, and MR are secondary tools here.
key_points: CT angiography aorta arch to iliac is the primary diagnostic
Rate control first (target HR below 60) then vasodilator
Stanford A requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery
explanation.pearls: A blood pressure difference of more than 20 mmHg between arms in a patient with tearing chest or back pain has a specificity above 80 percent for dissection; get the CT before starting anticoagulant or antiplatelet.

You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman transferred from a nursing home with 8 hours of fevers, rigors, and reduced oral intake. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and a permanent indwelling urinary catheter for neurogenic bladder. On arrival her Glasgow Coma Scale is 14, she is confused about place, and she has cool mottled knees.

Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 39.2. Point of care venous lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). Bedside creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90) from a rise of 82 last month. Urinalysis of catheter urine is grossly turbid with leucocytes 4+ and nitrites positive. Chest x-ray shows no consolidation. Two intravenous cannulas are in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/48, RR 26, SpO2 94% 4L NP, temp 39.2
data_table.qSOFA / signs: Altered mentation; SBP below 100; RR above 22
data_table.Bloods: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (from 82 last month)
data_table.Source clues: Turbid catheter urine; leucocytes 4+; nitrites positive; CXR clear

lead_in: Within the first hour of recognition, which sequence best reflects the ANZICS-endorsed sepsis bundle?

options.text: Give empirical antibiotics, then start intravenous fluids, then collect blood cultures once stable
options.rationale: Cultures should precede antibiotics whenever they do not delay antibiotic administration; collecting after antibiotics reduces yield and undermines antimicrobial stewardship (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Measure lactate, give a 500 mL fluid bolus, arrange CT abdomen, then collect blood cultures before antibiotics
options.rationale: Imaging is important for source control but delaying antibiotics for CT in confirmed septic shock breaches the hour-1 bundle; imaging follows initial resuscitation and antibiotics (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Measure lactate, collect blood cultures, give empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and commence 30 mL per kg crystalloid
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle groups lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics, empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and 30 mL per kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, delivered within the first hour of recognition (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Start noradrenaline infusion immediately then collect cultures and give antibiotics after stabilisation
options.rationale: Vasopressors are indicated after adequate fluid resuscitation for persistent hypotension; starting them before fluid loading is not standard bundle sequencing (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Commence 250 mL of 4 percent albumin, transfuse packed red cells for haemoglobin above 100, then give antibiotics
options.rationale: Crystalloid is the recommended initial resuscitation fluid; routine transfusion above 100 is not indicated (target above 70 unless active bleeding or myocardial ischaemia) (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle, endorsed by ANZICS, groups four actions within the first hour of sepsis recognition: measure lactate, collect blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not cause delay, administer empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and give 30 mL per kg crystalloid when there is hypotension or a lactate at or above 4 mmol/L. Vasopressors follow if mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mmHg after fluid loading. Imaging for source control (CT abdomen, ultrasound biliary tree) is important but sits after the initial four bundle elements. Catheter removal or exchange for a suspected catheter associated urinary sepsis is a specific source control step for this patient.
key_points: Bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid in the first hour
Vasopressors after fluid loading if MAP remains below 65 mmHg
Source control (catheter exchange, imaging) follows the initial bundle
explanation.pearls: In catheter associated urinary sepsis the indwelling catheter is the reservoir; a fresh catheter change (or removal where feasible) after the first antibiotic dose materially reduces bacterial load.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning a course of electroconvulsive therapy for a 68 year old woman with severe treatment resistant depression (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale 32) who has stopped eating and lost 12 percent body weight over 2 months. She has failed sequential trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine and lithium augmentation. She has a history of atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, hypertension on perindopril, and had a coronary artery bypass graft 5 years ago. Her most recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 52 percent.

She had an anterior circulation ischaemic stroke 4 weeks ago with complete recovery of neurological function. Her partner has consented on her behalf under the Mental Health Act after a formal capacity assessment. Vital signs are pulse 78 regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C.

data_table.Depression severity: HDRS 32; 12 percent weight loss in 2 months; stopped eating
data_table.Cardiac history: AF on apixaban; CABG 5 years ago; EF 52 percent
data_table.Recent event: Anterior circulation ischaemic stroke 4 weeks ago, complete recovery
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 148/86, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate action before proceeding with ECT?

options.text: Cancel the ECT course permanently because recent ischaemic stroke is an absolute contraindication
options.rationale: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT; recent stroke is a relative one that raises risk. Deferring rather than cancelling is the standard position when depression is severe (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Continue apixaban unchanged as it does not increase risk during ECT and requires no perioperative planning
options.rationale: Apixaban is generally continued for ECT because the procedure is very low bleeding risk, but this ignores the more pressing recent stroke issue that dominates decision making here (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Substitute intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with sertraline 200 mg orally as an alternative treatment plan
options.rationale: She has failed the antidepressant sequence already and adding olanzapine does not address the severe depression with life threatening malnutrition; alternatives do not match ECT for severity of this magnitude (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Proceed with ECT tomorrow because delaying more than 4 weeks after stroke removes the elevated risk
options.rationale: The recommended interval after a stroke is at least 4 to 6 weeks with cardiovascular and neurology review to define residual deficit and blood pressure control; going ahead the next day without that review is premature (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Defer ECT until at least 4 to 6 weeks post stroke with cardiology and neurology review of risk
options.rationale: Recent ischaemic stroke is a relative contraindication; RANZCP recommends deferring at least 4 to 6 weeks and obtaining specialist assessment of stroke risk with strict perioperative blood pressure targets before proceeding (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

explanation.summary: ECT has no absolute contraindications, but recent stroke, raised intracranial pressure, unstable coronary syndrome, aortic aneurysm, retinal detachment, phaeochromocytoma, and severe pulmonary disease are relative contraindications requiring risk assessment and modification. For an ischaemic stroke, RANZCP position statement PS28 recommends deferring ECT for at least 4 to 6 weeks and obtaining neurology and cardiology review with strict perioperative blood pressure control. Anticoagulants such as apixaban are usually continued because the procedure is very low bleeding risk. When severe depression demands ECT sooner, informed decision by treating team and patient (or substitute decision maker) is documented after formal risk balancing.
key_points: No absolute contraindications; recent stroke is relative
Defer at least 4 to 6 weeks after ischaemic stroke
Obtain neurology and cardiology review pre-anaesthesia
explanation.pearls: During ECT, systolic pressure can spike above 200 mmHg for seconds; premedication with a short acting beta blocker such as esmolol blunts the surge in patients with cardiovascular disease.

You are the outpatient psychiatry registrar seeing a 24 year old woman with bipolar I disorder currently well on sodium valproate 1000 mg orally twice daily for 3 years, and lithium was previously stopped for polyuria. She has had no manic or depressive episodes for 26 months and is engaged to be married. She and her partner would like to start trying to conceive in the next 12 months. She has never previously discussed contraception with her psychiatrist. Her partner uses condoms inconsistently.

Her weight is 74 kg, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and full blood count, electrolytes, and liver function tests are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects. She is very concerned that any change in medication will trigger a relapse and asks what to do next.

data_table.Current medication: Sodium valproate 1000 mg twice daily for 3 years
data_table.Mood stability: No manic or depressive episodes for 26 months
data_table.Contraception: Condoms used inconsistently by partner only

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Refer urgently for perinatal psychiatry review to plan a switch to a safer mood stabiliser preconception
options.rationale: Valproate causes major congenital malformation in 10 percent and neurodevelopmental impairment in 30 to 40 percent of exposed pregnancies; TGA guidance mandates a documented pregnancy prevention plan and specialist review for any woman of childbearing potential (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and add high dose folate 5 mg daily until conception
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not offset valproate teratogenicity and continuing valproate without discussion of alternatives fails the pregnancy prevention program (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly today and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated over the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks acute relapse; switch should be gradual under specialist supervision with careful cross titration and monitoring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue valproate but add long acting reversible contraception until she stops planning pregnancy
options.rationale: LARC is essential during ongoing valproate therapy, but she plans to conceive within 12 months so the aim is a preconception switch, not indefinite contraception (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg twice daily to lower teratogenic risk and continue at this dose during pregnancy
options.rationale: Teratogenic risk is dose related but even lower doses carry unacceptable risk versus alternatives; the plan is to switch off valproate preconception, not to reduce dose (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

explanation.summary: The TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program (2023) requires that any woman of childbearing potential prescribed valproate has documented understanding of teratogenic risk, effective contraception, an annual review, and a plan for pregnancy that involves an alternative mood stabiliser. Valproate carries a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation (including neural tube defects) and a 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment, well above lamotrigine (2 to 3 percent) or lithium (2 to 3 percent). The immediate step for a woman planning conception within 12 months is urgent specialist review to plan a gradual switch, not folate, dose reduction, or long term LARC on unchanged therapy.
key_points: Valproate MCM risk 10 percent; neurodevelopmental risk 30 to 40 percent
TGA program requires contraception plus annual review
Preconception switch to lamotrigine or lithium with specialist supervision
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine dose typically needs to be doubled by the third trimester because oestrogen induces UGT glucuronidation; drop back to preconception dose within 3 days post partum.

You are the medical registrar coordinating care for a 58 year old man with cirrhosis brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 4 hour history of vomiting fresh red blood. He has vomited 3 more times since arrival, each estimated 300 to 400 mL. Ambulance recorded blood pressure 82/48 mmHg and pulse 128 with two 16 gauge cannulas placed en route and 1000 mL of Hartmann's solution infused.

On arrival pulse 132, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees C. He is confused (GCS 13) and peripheries are cold. Bedside haemoglobin 62 g/L (135 to 175), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150 to 400), INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L (2.0 to 4.0), lactate 6.8 mmol/L. You have called endoscopy and given intravenous terlipressin and ceftriaxone. Two units of emergency O negative packed cells are already infusing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 78/44, RR 26, SpO2 96% 4L NP, temp 35.4, GCS 13
data_table.Prior resuscitation: 1000 mL Hartmann's; 2 units emergency O negative pRBC infusing

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his resuscitation?

options.text: Continue two more units of O negative packed cells and reassess response after another 500 mL Hartmann's
options.rationale: Ongoing crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia; empirical continuation of packed cells alone will not correct the fibrinogen or coagulopathy that will drive continued bleeding (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol and target packed cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate
options.rationale: ANZ National Blood Authority guidance recommends MTP activation for critical bleeding likely to require 5 or more units in 4 hours, or a shock index above 1 with ongoing haemorrhage; balanced replacement of pRBC, FFP, platelets, and cryoprecipitate corrects coagulopathy and reduces mortality (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Give a single unit of platelets alone since platelet count is only mildly reduced at 68 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Isolated platelet transfusion does not correct the coagulopathy, hypofibrinogenaemia, and ongoing loss; balanced product resuscitation is required (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Give intravenous prothrombinex 25 units per kg to correct INR of 2.1 in place of any plasma or platelets
options.rationale: Prothrombinex is a factor concentrate for warfarin or DOAC related bleeding; it does not replace fibrinogen or platelets and is not the correct product for critical bleeding coagulopathy (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Delay further transfusion until formal cross match is complete to reduce the risk of a haemolytic reaction
options.rationale: In critical bleeding with ongoing shock, emergency group O red cells and MTP components are given without waiting for cross match; the risk of exsanguination exceeds the risk of an unmatched transfusion (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

explanation.summary: The Australian National Blood Authority defines critical bleeding as major haemorrhage that is life threatening and likely to require massive transfusion (5 or more units of red cells in 4 hours). Activation of the massive transfusion protocol triggers balanced delivery of packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate, aiming for physiological targets (temperature above 35 degrees C, pH above 7.2, ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L, fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, platelets above 50 to 100 depending on setting, INR less than 1.5). Tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours reduces mortality in trauma; in upper GI bleeding evidence is less strong but is often used. Definitive source control (endoscopy, angiography, surgery) is the definitive step.
key_points: MTP for 5+ units in 4 hours or shock plus ongoing haemorrhage
Balanced pRBC, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate
Physiological targets: temp above 35, pH above 7.2, iCa above 1.1
explanation.pearls: Ionised calcium falls rapidly with citrated products; replace with 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate for every 4 units of blood product to prevent bleeding from citrate hypocalcaemia.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion
