You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52 year old man in outpatients 3 months after a right sided segmental pulmonary embolus. There was no preceding surgery, plaster cast, prolonged immobility, hospitalisation, cancer, oestrogen exposure, or long haul travel. He has no personal or family history of thrombosis. His pulmonary embolism was diagnosed on CT pulmonary angiogram after 3 days of pleuritic chest pain; troponin was negative and echocardiogram normal. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis.

Repeat compression ultrasound of the legs is normal. D-dimer measured today after 4 weeks off treatment (planned trial cessation) is 620 micrograms/L (less than 500). Full blood count, renal function, liver function tests, and coagulation studies are within normal limits. He is a non-smoker, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, has hypertension controlled with perindopril, and works as a physiotherapist. His HAS-BLED score is 1.

data_table.Anticoagulant: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis
data_table.Post-cessation trial D-dimer: 620 micrograms/L (less than 500) after 4 weeks off treatment

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from this point?

options.text: Stop apixaban permanently now and rely on daily 100 mg aspirin as long term secondary prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for secondary prevention of unprovoked VTE and stopping anticoagulation with a positive post-cessation D-dimer risks recurrence at 5 to 10 percent per year (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely without dose reduction at any point in the future
options.rationale: Extended therapy is warranted, but current evidence supports dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months for unprovoked VTE with acceptable bleeding profile (AMPLIFY-EXT); indefinite full dose is not the preferred plan (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Extend apixaban for a further 3 months only then reassess with repeat D-dimer at that time again
options.rationale: A finite additional course does not resolve the ongoing recurrence risk in unprovoked VTE with a positive D-dimer; recurrence risk after any finite duration returns to baseline once anticoagulation stops (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months as extended low intensity secondary prevention
options.rationale: For unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk and features suggesting persistent risk (positive post-cessation D-dimer), THANZ endorses extended anticoagulation, with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months preferred over full dose per AMPLIFY-EXT data (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2 to 3 for at least 10 years then reassess bleeding risk
options.rationale: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for extended VTE therapy in the absence of specific indications (antiphospholipid syndrome, severe renal impairment); switching without cause adds monitoring burden and bleeding risk (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

explanation.summary: Unprovoked pulmonary embolism carries an annual recurrence risk of about 5 to 10 percent per year once anticoagulation stops after a standard 3 to 6 month course. THANZ recommends extended anticoagulation for unprovoked proximal DVT or PE where bleeding risk is acceptable, and the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months, which preserves efficacy against recurrence with lower bleeding rates than full dose. A positive post-cessation D-dimer after 4 weeks off treatment strongly favours continued therapy in this scenario. Aspirin is inferior to DOAC. Warfarin is preferred only for antiphospholipid syndrome and severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 30).
key_points: Unprovoked VTE recurrence 5 to 10 percent per year after stopping
Extended apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is preferred beyond 6 months
Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for extended secondary prevention
explanation.pearls: A positive D-dimer 4 weeks after stopping anticoagulation carries a hazard ratio of about 2 for recurrent VTE and is a legitimate discriminator when extending therapy is uncertain.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic discrimination among short duration psychoses
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 22 year old university student 3 weeks after his acute admission for hearing derogatory voices, believing his housemates were poisoning his water, and 4 days of not sleeping. He had never before had psychiatric contact. On admission urine drug screen was negative and MRI brain was unremarkable. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg nightly and voices and delusions resolved within 8 days; sleep normalised.

He was discharged home after 12 days with complete symptom resolution. He remains well today with no residual positive or negative symptoms. Total duration of psychotic symptoms from onset to full resolution was 12 days. He has no family history of psychotic illness, no substance use in the last 6 months confirmed by hair testing at admission, and no recent bereavement or trauma. He asks what the diagnostic label is now.

data_table.Symptom duration: 12 days total from onset to resolution
data_table.Response: Complete resolution on olanzapine 10 mg within 8 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic label at this stage?

options.text: Schizophrenia with active phase symptoms controlled by second generation antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least 6 months including active phase symptoms of at least 1 month; a 12 day episode does not meet criteria (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder with good prognostic features and complete symptom resolution on therapy
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms for at least 1 month but less than 6 months; a 12 day episode does not reach the 1 month threshold (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with symptom duration between 1 day and 1 month with return to prior functioning
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder in DSM-5 requires at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month with eventual full return to premorbid functioning; a 12 day episode meets this criterion exactly (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder related to unreported hallucinogen exposure prior to admission
options.rationale: A substance induced diagnosis requires temporal linkage to intoxication or withdrawal and evidence of substance exposure; UDS was negative and hair testing did not support recent use (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Delusional disorder with persecutory type since his beliefs about being poisoned were the dominant feature
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires delusions for at least 1 month without prominent hallucinations, mood disturbance, or bizarre behaviour; hallucinations are prominent here and duration is under 1 month (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 discriminates short duration psychoses by two axes: symptom duration and functional recovery. Brief psychotic disorder requires 1 day to less than 1 month with full return to premorbid functioning. Schizophreniform disorder covers 1 month to less than 6 months. Schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous disturbance including 1 month of active phase symptoms. Delusional disorder requires delusions of 1 month or more without prominent hallucinations, mood disturbance, or bizarre behaviour. Substance induced psychotic disorder requires temporal linkage and evidence of substance exposure. In this 12 day episode with full resolution, brief psychotic disorder is the correct provisional diagnosis; recurrence would trigger reclassification.
key_points: Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day to less than 1 month with full recovery
Schizophreniform: 1 to less than 6 months
Schizophrenia: 6 months continuous with 1 month active phase
explanation.pearls: About 50 percent of brief psychotic disorder episodes progress to another psychotic diagnosis over 5 years; longitudinal follow up rather than a definitive label is the safer position early on.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the emergency department attending a 34 year old woman brought in by police after threatening staff at a supermarket. She is known to services with schizoaffective disorder, currently on paliperidone long acting injection given 5 weeks ago. She is pacing, shouting, and refusing all oral medications. Verbal de-escalation over 15 minutes has been unsuccessful. She has no known allergies, is not pregnant (bhCG negative from urine), has never had NMS, and is otherwise physically well.

Vital signs (obtained during a brief cooperative moment) are pulse 108, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Point of care glucose 6.2 mmol/L. Weight is estimated at 65 kg. Security officers and 4 nursing staff are present. There is no intravenous access.

data_table.Presentation: Agitated, pacing, verbally threatening; refuses oral medication
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 138/86, RR 22, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial parenteral pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg alone as monotherapy without concurrent benzodiazepine at this time
options.rationale: The RANZCP and eTG rapid tranquillisation position places IM olanzapine 10 mg monotherapy as first line for acute behavioural disturbance in known psychosis; avoid concurrent IM benzodiazepine to reduce respiratory depression risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg concurrently with intramuscular midazolam 5 mg into the same deltoid muscle
options.rationale: Combined IM droperidol and IM midazolam increases risk of respiratory depression and hypotension and is not the first line combination; same site injection is also poor technique (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with promethazine 50 mg in a single deltoid muscle injection
options.rationale: Haloperidol 10 mg carries higher extrapyramidal risk than lower doses; combined with promethazine 50 mg the anticholinergic burden and QT risk make this a second line rather than first choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular ziprasidone 20 mg pending intravenous access for potential propofol induction if needed
options.rationale: Ziprasidone is not widely available in Australia, and moving toward propofol induction without a trial of first line IM options is unnecessarily invasive (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg per kg as a single dose to achieve immediate dissociative sedation onset
options.rationale: Ketamine dissociative sedation is a prehospital or resistant restraint option; it is not the initial pharmacological choice in the emergency department with staff and safer options available (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Australian rapid tranquillisation guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP position) recommends verbal de-escalation and oral options first; when parenteral therapy is needed, intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg is a first line monotherapy for known psychosis, or intramuscular droperidol 10 mg. Concurrent IM benzodiazepines are avoided due to risk of respiratory depression. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring with pulse oximetry for at least 1 hour follows any dose, plus glucose check within 30 minutes. If the initial dose is inadequate, repeat after 30 to 60 minutes rather than stacking multiple agents. Vital signs, glucose, ECG for QT, and search for reversible causes (hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, drug or alcohol intoxication) are essential adjuncts.
key_points: IM olanzapine 10 mg or IM droperidol 10 mg first line monotherapy
Avoid concurrent IM benzodiazepine (respiratory depression risk)
Monitor SpO2, pulse, BP, glucose after every dose
explanation.pearls: Do not repeat IM olanzapine within 2 hours; peak concentrations at 15 to 45 minutes mean early re-dosing risks cumulative sedation and hypotension.

subtopic_detail: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 46 year old man with 5 days of unsteady gait and double vision. He had 3 days of gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago (self limited, no antibiotics). On examination he is alert with normal cognition. Cranial nerve examination shows bilateral partial abduction failure with limitation of upgaze; pupils are 4 mm and sluggishly reactive. Facial strength and swallow are normal. Limb power is 5 out of 5 throughout with normal tone; deep tendon reflexes are absent at both biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles. Plantar responses are downgoing.

Romberg positive; heel-shin dysmetria bilaterally. Vital signs are pulse 82 regular, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C. Bedside single breath count is 32; forced vital capacity 4.1 L. MRI brain and orbits are unremarkable. CSF from lumbar puncture shows protein 0.9 g/L (0.15 to 0.45), white cell count 3 x10^6/L (less than 5), glucose 3.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Peripheral: Areflexia; power 5/5; sensory loss absent; Romberg positive
data_table.CSF: Protein 0.9 g/L; WCC 3 x10^6/L; glucose 3.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which single specific antibody test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Anti aquaporin 4 antibody serum titre to distinguish neuromyelitis optica spectrum from other syndromes
options.rationale: Aquaporin 4 antibodies characterise neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, typically with optic neuritis or transverse myelitis, not ophthalmoplegia with areflexia (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti acetylcholine receptor antibody assay to confirm myasthenia gravis at a specialised neuroimmunology lab
options.rationale: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies confirm generalised myasthenia gravis, but the areflexia and CSF albuminocytological dissociation here point away from myasthenia (reflexes are preserved) (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody to characterise a demyelinating central nervous system syndrome
options.rationale: MOG antibodies mark central demyelinating disease and are not associated with the ophthalmoplegia and areflexia pattern of Miller Fisher syndrome (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti GQ1b IgG serum antibody to confirm the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
options.rationale: Anti GQ1b IgG is present in over 85 percent of Miller Fisher syndrome, characterised by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after a preceding infection; the triad plus CSF albuminocytological dissociation fits classically (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti Hu paraneoplastic antibody panel to look for an underlying small cell lung cancer in the setting
options.rationale: Anti Hu antibodies are associated with paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy and encephalomyelitis, not the acute post infective Miller Fisher pattern (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome is a Guillain-Barre variant defined by the triad of external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after an infective prodrome, most commonly Campylobacter jejuni or upper respiratory viruses. Anti GQ1b IgG is present in over 85 percent of cases and is the most specific serological confirmation. CSF classically shows albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein with normal white cell count) after the first week. Management is IVIG or plasma exchange with close respiratory monitoring; vital capacity below 20 mL per kg or negative inspiratory force above -30 cmH2O predicts need for ventilation. Miller Fisher generally has a good prognosis with recovery over weeks to months.
key_points: Triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia
Anti GQ1b IgG in more than 85 percent of Miller Fisher cases
Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange with close respiratory monitoring
explanation.pearls: Single breath count under 20 or a falling forced vital capacity in Guillain-Barre spectrum disease warrants ICU review even before oxygen desaturation; respiratory failure is often abrupt.

stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 74 year old woman with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis maintained on warfarin 5 mg on alternate days with 4 mg on the other days for the past 6 years. She takes no other regular medications. She rings you because a routine INR taken today shows 8.9 (target 2.5 to 3.5 for mechanical mitral valve). She feels well, has no bruising, no gum bleeding, no melaena, no haematuria, and no headache. She reports she started a 5 day course of clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily 4 days ago for a chest infection.

Baseline vital signs 2 weeks ago were pulse 72 regular, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, and today she reports feeling the same. She has an appointment available with her cardiologist next week and lives 15 minutes drive from a public hospital emergency department. She asks what to do now.

data_table.Warfarin regimen: 5 mg on alternate days with 4 mg on other days for 6 years
data_table.Recent medication: Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily started 4 days ago
data_table.Bleeding: No overt bleeding or headache reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue current warfarin dose and repeat INR in 2 weeks after clarithromycin course completes
options.rationale: An INR above 8 carries a high risk of spontaneous bleeding; continuing warfarin without action is unsafe even without overt bleeding (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous vitamin K 10 mg via slow infusion at home to reverse anticoagulation now
options.rationale: IV vitamin K is reserved for major bleeding and can fully reverse anticoagulation, which is undesirable in a patient with a mechanical mitral valve; oral low dose vitamin K is preferred for asymptomatic elevation (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Administer prothrombinex 25 units per kg with fresh frozen plasma at the general practice today
options.rationale: Prothrombinex is reserved for major or life threatening bleeding, or urgent surgery; use in asymptomatic elevation risks over correction and thrombosis around a mechanical valve (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Withhold two warfarin doses only, without vitamin K, and repeat INR in 3 days at the practice
options.rationale: For INR above 8 without bleeding, guidance is to withhold warfarin and give 1 to 2 mg oral vitamin K; withholding alone is inadequate (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Withhold warfarin, give 1 mg oral vitamin K1 (phytomenadione), and repeat INR in 24 hours
options.rationale: For INR above 8 without significant bleeding, National Blood Authority guidance recommends withholding warfarin and giving 1 to 2 mg oral vitamin K; the mechanical valve makes over correction with high dose IV vitamin K undesirable (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

explanation.summary: National Blood Authority warfarin reversal guidance stratifies management by INR level and bleeding. INR above target but below 4.5 with no bleeding: reduce dose or omit next dose. INR 4.5 to 10 with no bleeding: withhold warfarin, consider 1 mg oral vitamin K if bleeding risk is high. INR above 10 with no bleeding: withhold warfarin, give 3 to 5 mg oral vitamin K. Any INR with major bleeding: prothrombinex 25 to 50 units per kg plus fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL plus 5 to 10 mg IV vitamin K. In this scenario with INR 8.9 and no bleeding, oral low dose vitamin K 1 mg with warfarin withholding is the fit. Also stop the interacting antibiotic (clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, raising warfarin levels).
key_points: INR 4.5 to 10 no bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
INR above 10 no bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg
Major bleeding: prothrombinex plus FFP plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg
explanation.pearls: Clarithromycin, erythromycin, metronidazole, fluconazole, and amiodarone all raise INR through CYP inhibition; check INR within 3 to 5 days of starting or stopping them if patient is on warfarin.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

subtopic_detail: Cannabis induced vs primary psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 19 year old man 6 weeks after admission for auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions. On admission urine drug screen was positive for THC only, and hair testing at 3 cm covered the preceding 3 months and was positive for high potency cannabis (used 3 to 5 times daily). He was started on risperidone 2 mg twice daily and voices resolved by day 4.

He has been abstinent from cannabis since discharge (confirmed by weekly urine drug screens, all negative for 6 weeks) and remains on risperidone 2 mg twice daily. He still reports intermittent low grade suspiciousness and hears his name called once or twice weekly, though he is otherwise functioning at work and university. He has no family history of psychotic illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4) and prolactin 780 mIU/L (60 to 620) are within normal limits and mildly elevated respectively.

data_table.Substance use: Abstinent 6 weeks (weekly UDS negative); prior heavy high potency use

lead_in: What does the persistence of these symptoms most strongly suggest?

options.text: Reasonable expectation of substance induced psychotic disorder that will resolve with more time abstinent
options.rationale: DSM-5 substance induced psychotic disorder should resolve within a month of cessation of the substance; persistence beyond a month suggests reclassification (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Primary psychotic disorder in the schizophrenia spectrum with cannabis acting as an environmental trigger
options.rationale: Positive symptoms persisting 6 weeks after cannabis cessation exceed the 1 month cut off for substance induced psychosis; DSM-5 and RANZCP guidance treat this as an emerging primary psychotic disorder with cannabis as a precipitant, not the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Prolactinoma related psychosis given the modestly elevated prolactin of 780 mIU/L on risperidone therapy
options.rationale: Elevated prolactin on risperidone is a medication effect (D2 blockade); prolactinoma related psychosis is not a recognised entity and does not explain his symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Ongoing covert cannabis use with false negative urine drug screens each week from insufficient sensitivity
options.rationale: Weekly UDS is highly reliable for detecting cannabis use over the preceding week in an abstinent user; sustained negatives over 6 weeks make continued use very unlikely (Source: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position).
source_refs: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position

options.text: Persistent hallucinogen perception disorder from previous LSD use rather than cannabis specific effects here
options.rationale: Persistent perception disorder is visual and follows classical hallucinogen use; auditory hallucinations after cannabis use do not fit this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 substance induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms arise during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal and resolve within a month of cessation. Symptoms lasting beyond this period despite confirmed abstinence should be reclassified as a primary psychotic disorder, most often schizophrenia spectrum, with cannabis acting as an important environmental trigger. Heavy high potency cannabis use in adolescence multiplies the risk of schizophrenia several fold. Ongoing antipsychotic therapy and specialist follow up are appropriate; prolactin elevation on risperidone is dose related and monitored, not diagnostic of a separate condition. Weekly urine cannabis screening is reliable for confirming abstinence over the preceding week in a previously heavy user.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis resolves within 1 month of cessation
Persistence beyond 1 month reclassifies to a primary psychotic disorder
Heavy adolescent cannabis use multiplies schizophrenia risk
explanation.pearls: Cannabis withdrawal alone can produce sleep disturbance and irritability for weeks but does not sustain positive psychotic symptoms; new hallucinations at 6 weeks abstinent point at a primary disorder.

sources.label: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position

stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38 year old firefighter with 8 months of intrusive daily flashbacks and nightmares following a motor vehicle accident he attended where three people died. He avoids driving past the accident site, is hypervigilant to sirens, has developed insomnia, and lost interest in weekend sport. His PCL-5 score is 46. He drinks 6 standard drinks on Friday and Saturday evenings only; he has no personal or family history of psychotic illness or bipolar disorder.

His Clinician Administered PTSD Scale confirms DSM-5 PTSD diagnosis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Full blood count, TSH, and fasting glucose are unremarkable. His wife has separated from him and they have two young children he sees on weekends. He is currently on no psychotropic medication and asks specifically about talking therapies rather than tablets. He can commit to weekly attendance for 3 months.

data_table.Symptom duration: 8 months of intrusive daily flashbacks and nightmares
data_table.Alcohol: 6 standard drinks Friday and Saturday only

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate primary psychological intervention to recommend now?

options.text: Non directive supportive counselling delivered weekly by a Medicare mental health social worker for 12 sessions
options.rationale: Supportive counselling has limited efficacy for established PTSD; trauma focused therapies achieve larger effect sizes and are the recommended first line (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Psychoanalytic psychotherapy exploring childhood attachment patterns over 6 to 12 months of weekly sessions
options.rationale: Psychoanalytic psychotherapy is not a recommended first line treatment for PTSD; Phoenix Australia recommends short focused trauma work over longer non focused approaches (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Trauma focused cognitive behaviour therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing across 8 to 12 sessions
options.rationale: Phoenix Australia's Australian Guidelines for PTSD recommend trauma focused CBT (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) and EMDR as first line psychological treatments for PTSD, delivered by trained clinicians (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Group debriefing single session for critical incident stress delivered within 72 hours of a related trauma trigger
options.rationale: Single session critical incident debriefing does not prevent PTSD and may worsen outcomes in some studies; it has no role in established PTSD management (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Mindfulness only meditation practice via a downloadable app self directed for 8 weeks without clinician contact
options.rationale: App based mindfulness alone is not sufficient for established PTSD; it may be a helpful adjunct but not the primary intervention (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

explanation.summary: Phoenix Australia's Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD, and Complex PTSD recommend trauma focused cognitive behaviour therapy (including prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy) and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) as first line psychological treatments for adults with PTSD, delivered by trained clinicians typically over 8 to 12 weekly sessions. Pharmacotherapy with sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine is a first line pharmacological option and is considered when trauma focused therapy is not accessible, declined, or partially effective. Non specific supportive counselling and single session debriefing have limited or negative evidence.
key_points: First line: TF-CBT (prolonged exposure, CPT) or EMDR
Typical course 8 to 12 weekly sessions by trained clinician
SSRI or SNRI first line pharmacotherapy where indicated
explanation.pearls: Alcohol use commonly complicates PTSD; brief intervention on hazardous drinking should accompany the trauma focused work rather than delay it.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition and surgical urgency
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63 year old man admitted 6 hours ago with a red painful right lower leg after minor gardening trauma 24 hours earlier. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. Since arrival his pain has escalated from 4 out of 10 to 9 out of 10 despite oral oxycodone 15 mg and paracetamol 1 g given 90 minutes ago. He now has a tense, waxy area of swelling above the ankle with 2 haemorrhagic bullae, and the skin overlying appears anaesthetic to pinprick testing.

Vital signs deteriorate: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C. Bloods: white cell count 22 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), sodium 129 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 178 micromol/L (from 92 last month), glucose 14.2 mmol/L, CRP 348 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 4.4 mmol/L. His LRINEC score is calculated at 9.

data_table.Local findings: Tense waxy swelling; 2 haemorrhagic bullae; skin anaesthesia to pinprick
data_table.Pain trajectory: Escalated from 4/10 to 9/10 despite opioid analgesia
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 96% RA, temp 39.4

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate step in management?

options.text: Give intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and admit for 48 hours of observation before reassessment
options.rationale: Empirical monotherapy for streptococcal cellulitis alone underdoses necrotising fasciitis and delays the essential surgical review; broader empirical cover plus urgent surgery is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before surgical review
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical diagnosis; MRI can delay definitive debridement and false negatives occur early. Imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Elevate the limb, apply topical dressings, and mark the erythematous margin for reassessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Standard cellulitis nursing measures are inadequate for suspected necrotising fasciitis; delay of a few hours can be lethal and progression is rapid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Urgent surgical referral for operative exploration with concurrent broad spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation
options.rationale: LRINEC score 9 with anaesthetic skin, haemorrhagic bullae, and pain out of proportion has very high probability of necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement with concurrent broad spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin) is the definitive first step (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Refer to hyperbaric oxygen therapy after intravenous antibiotics have been running for 24 hours
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen may be an adjunct after debridement in some centres but is not the immediate step and must not delay surgery (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where every hour of delay increases mortality (which reaches 25 to 30 percent overall). Clinical clues that separate it from severe cellulitis are pain out of proportion to visible findings, anaesthetic skin over the affected area, haemorrhagic or dusky bullae, rapid progression, and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose to stratify risk; a score of 6 or more is intermediate risk and 8 or more high risk. Empirical antibiotics are piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin (for antitoxin effect against group A strep) plus vancomycin (for MRSA). Definitive management is urgent operative debridement; imaging must not delay surgical review.
key_points: Surgical debridement is definitive and time critical
LRINEC score 6 to 8 intermediate risk, 8 or more high risk
Empirical: piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin
explanation.pearls: Anaesthesia over the affected skin from cutaneous nerve destruction is a late but highly specific sign; if you find it, the patient is going to theatre now.

stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 72 year old postmenopausal woman 8 weeks after a wrist fracture sustained from a fall from standing height. She has no significant medical history, no current medications, and is a lifelong non smoker. Her mother had a hip fracture aged 75. DXA scan shows lumbar spine T score -2.1 and femoral neck T score -2.6.

Vitamin D was 62 nmol/L (above 50), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60), TSH within normal limits, and eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73m2. Coeliac serology is negative and full blood count and myeloma screen are unremarkable. She has good dentition and no recent dental work planned. She drinks 1 standard drink weekly and walks 30 minutes daily. She asks what medication is best to reduce her risk of another fracture.

data_table.Fracture history: Left distal radius fracture 8 weeks ago from fall from standing height
data_table.DXA: Lumbar spine T -2.1; femoral neck T -2.6
data_table.Bloods: Vitamin D 62 nmol/L; corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L; eGFR 74; TSH within normal limits
data_table.Secondary screen: Coeliac serology negative; myeloma screen normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy to recommend now?

options.text: Calcium 1000 mg with vitamin D 1000 IU daily as a single agent for 12 months and reassess DXA scan
options.rationale: Calcium plus vitamin D alone does not adequately reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis with a minimal trauma fracture; specific antiresorptive therapy is required (Source: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide).
source_refs: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide

options.text: Subcutaneous romosozumab 210 mg monthly for 12 months as anabolic agent for very high risk profile
options.rationale: Romosozumab is reserved for very high fracture risk profiles (multiple fractures, very low T score); first line here is oral bisphosphonate, and romosozumab carries cardiovascular caution (Source: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide).
source_refs: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms daily for 24 months as an anabolic agent first line
options.rationale: Teriparatide is a second line PBS restricted anabolic for severe osteoporosis where bisphosphonate has failed or is contraindicated; it is not first line here (Source: PBS Teriparatide Listing).

options.text: Oestrogen with progestogen menopausal hormone therapy for prevention of further fragility fracture
options.rationale: Menopausal hormone therapy is reserved for symptomatic postmenopausal women in the first 10 years after menopause; it is not first line for osteoporosis in a 72 year old (Source: RACGP Menopausal Hormone Therapy Guidance).

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation as first line therapy
options.rationale: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is first line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture in an ambulant patient with normal renal function and good dentition; PBS covers it after a minimal trauma fracture (Source: PBS Alendronate Listing).

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman with T score below -2.5 defines osteoporosis and mandates specific antiresorptive therapy in addition to calcium and vitamin D. Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly (or risedronate 35 mg weekly) is first line where renal function is preserved (eGFR above 30 for oral, above 35 for zoledronic acid) and gastro-oesophageal reflux is not prohibitive. Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenous annually is an alternative for adherence or reflux concerns. Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous six monthly is second line and requires uninterrupted therapy (rebound fractures on cessation). Teriparatide and romosozumab are reserved for severe or very high risk cases via PBS restriction. Vitamin D above 50 nmol/L should be maintained and calcium intake at 1200 to 1300 mg daily supported by diet plus supplementation where needed.
key_points: Fragility fracture plus T below -2.5 defines pharmacotherapy indication
Oral alendronate weekly is first line with normal renal function
Denosumab must not be stopped without transition to bisphosphonate
explanation.pearls: Vitamin D should be at or above 50 nmol/L before initiating a bisphosphonate; hypocalcaemia after zoledronic acid is common if vitamin D is deficient at baseline.

sources.label: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide

subtopic_detail: Uterine inversion diagnosis and immediate management
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite. A G3P2 at 39 weeks gestation has just delivered a healthy 3.9 kg baby vaginally. During active third stage management the midwife applied cord traction with 10 units of oxytocin already given intramuscularly at anterior shoulder delivery. She calls you urgently: the mother has become suddenly light headed, and the midwife feels a large mass in the vagina with no palpable uterine fundus on abdominal examination. Estimated blood loss is 900 mL and increasing at 100 mL every 2 minutes.

Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 74/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air. The placenta is partially separated but still attached to the mass. She has two 16 gauge intravenous cannulas with Hartmann's solution running wide open. Full theatre and anaesthetic teams have been called and are 5 minutes away. Blood is being cross matched.

data_table.Vaginal examination: Large firm mass in vagina; fundus absent abdominally
data_table.Blood loss: 900 mL rising at 100 mL every 2 minutes
data_table.Prior actions: 10 units IM oxytocin given at shoulder delivery; cord traction applied

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate step now?

options.text: Attempt immediate manual replacement of the inverted uterus with the placenta still attached
options.rationale: RANZCOG guidance calls for immediate manual repositioning (Johnson manoeuvre) without removing an adherent placenta first, since removal worsens haemorrhage; every minute of delay makes reduction harder as the cervical ring contracts (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Remove the placenta manually before any attempt at replacement to reduce weight of the inverted uterus
options.rationale: Manual removal of an attached placenta from an inverted uterus dramatically increases haemorrhage and is contraindicated before replacement (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Give intravenous carboprost 250 micrograms and misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally to control bleeding first
options.rationale: Uterotonics contract the cervical ring around the inversion and make reduction much harder; hold uterotonics until replacement is achieved (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Transfer the patient to theatre now for hysterectomy without any attempt at bedside replacement first
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is a last resort for irreducible inversion; almost all inversions reduce with prompt manual replacement, and hysterectomy without an attempt at replacement is not standard care (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Insert an intrauterine Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL to tamponade bleeding while awaiting theatre transfer
options.rationale: A Bakri balloon in an inverted uterus increases the inversion and is inappropriate; balloon tamponade has its role after replacement if atony persists (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion complicates 1 in 2000 to 1 in 20 000 deliveries and presents with a vaginal mass, absent fundus abdominally, sudden hypotension out of keeping with blood loss (vagal), and shock. The immediate step is manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre): the operator's cupped hand pushes the fundus back through the cervix with the placenta still attached, sustaining pressure for several minutes until the uterus contracts around the hand. Uterotonics are withheld until replacement is achieved because they trap the fundus; once replaced, oxytocin infusion helps maintain uterine tone. Under general anaesthesia with terbutaline, magnesium sulfate, or nitroglycerin uterine relaxation is used if bedside reduction fails. Massive transfusion protocol activation is concurrent.
key_points: Manual replacement with placenta still attached is first line
Hold uterotonics until replacement is achieved
Uterine relaxants under anaesthesia if bedside attempts fail
explanation.pearls: The vagal response to inversion (bradycardia and hypotension) may exceed the blood loss and mislead volume assessment; anticipate large fluid and blood requirements at replacement.

stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19 year old woman with anorexia nervosa restricting type. She weighs 39 kg at height 168 cm (BMI 13.8), has had no oral intake beyond 200 kcal daily for the last 4 weeks, and lost 12 kg over 6 months. Vital signs are pulse 42 supine and 68 standing (postural fall in systolic BP from 96 to 78 mmHg), respiratory rate 12, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 35.6 degrees C.

Bloods show sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.5), albumin 42 g/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 42 with corrected QT interval 458 ms. Full blood count and TSH are within normal limits. She is admitted to a specialist eating disorder ward.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 supine, 68 standing; postural BP fall 96/? to 78/?; RR 12; SpO2 99% RA; temp 35.6

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial nutritional and biochemical plan for the first 72 hours?

options.text: Commence full nutrition at 40 kcal per kg per day with no electrolyte supplementation until deficits become clinically evident
options.rationale: Full calorie loading of a severely malnourished patient rapidly triggers refeeding syndrome; guidelines call for a cautious start with proactive electrolyte replacement (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Feed at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day, give thiamine 200 mg orally daily, and give empirical phosphate, potassium, and magnesium replacement
options.rationale: MARSIPAN Australia and RANZCP guidance recommend cautious refeeding at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for the first 3 days, thiamine 200 mg daily before or with the first meal, and empirical phosphate, potassium, and magnesium supplementation with twice daily electrolyte checks (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refuse hospital admission and refer immediately to community outpatient dietitian for weekly weight and meal plan review
options.rationale: BMI below 14 with bradycardia and hypokalaemia meets criteria for medical admission; community management alone would be unsafe (Source: MARSIPAN Australia Guidance).

options.text: Start high dose intravenous glucose 10 percent at 100 mL per hour for 24 hours before any oral or nasogastric intake begins
options.rationale: Intravenous dextrose without thiamine and electrolyte replacement precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and severe refeeding hypophosphataemia (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Administer nasogastric feeding at 60 mL per hour of standard formula from admission with electrolytes replaced only if abnormal
options.rationale: Rapid nasogastric feeding rates deliver too many calories on the first day of a severely malnourished patient; slow escalation with prophylactic electrolyte replacement is required (Source: MARSIPAN Australia Guidance).

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa with BMI below 14, bradycardia below 50, hypokalaemia, or postural hypotension is a medical admission per MARSIPAN Australia and RANZCP eating disorder guidance. Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, fluid overload, cardiac failure, Wernicke encephalopathy) is prevented by starting calories at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for the first 3 days, giving thiamine 200 mg daily orally before feeds begin, and prescribing empirical replacement of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. Electrolytes are checked twice daily for the first 5 days and calories are escalated as tolerated. Cardiac monitoring is required for QTc above 500 ms or pulse below 40.
key_points: Start at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for first 3 days
Thiamine 200 mg daily before feeds; empirical PO4, K+, Mg replacement
Twice daily electrolytes for 5 days; cardiac monitoring for severe bradycardia
explanation.pearls: The MEED Australian tool (medical emergencies in eating disorders) sets specific thresholds for cardiac monitoring: pulse below 40, systolic BP below 90, QTc above 500 ms, or postural drop above 20 mmHg.

sources.label: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Early intervention in psychosis family involvement
stem:
You are the early psychosis service registrar reviewing a 20 year old university student 6 weeks after his first admission for schizophrenia. He is on aripiprazole 15 mg daily, positive symptoms have resolved, and he wants to return to living with his parents while he resumes engineering studies. His parents ask what they can do to reduce the chance of relapse. He consents to their involvement in his care.

He scores 4 on the PHQ-9, has no substance use, and family assessment shows warmth, but the father expresses high levels of criticism when his son does not respond immediately to requests. Mother is highly reassuring and takes over daily tasks he can manage. Both parents are anxious about future relapse and ask what to do at home. He agrees a family meeting would help. Vital signs and metabolic screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Recovery stage: 6 weeks post first admission; positive symptoms resolved
data_table.Family climate: Warmth present; father high critical comments; mother overinvolved

lead_in: Which family based intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing relapse in first episode psychosis?

options.text: Weekly individual supportive counselling for parents only, delivered separately from the patient
options.rationale: Individual parent counselling alone has less evidence than structured family intervention that includes the patient and addresses expressed emotion (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: A single family psychoeducation session at discharge covering illness basics and warning signs
options.rationale: One off sessions are insufficient; sustained multisession psychoeducation across 3 to 6 months is required to reduce relapse (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: Structured family intervention over 3 or more months addressing expressed emotion, problem solving, and psychoeducation
options.rationale: Meta analyses and RANZCP guidance find structured family intervention lasting 3 months or more, addressing expressed emotion (high criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement), problem solving skills, and psychoeducation reduces relapse by around 50 percent at 12 months (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: Referral of both parents to a chronic mental illness carer support group with peer led format only
options.rationale: Peer support groups are valuable adjuncts but have less evidence for relapse prevention than structured family intervention delivered by trained clinicians (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: Removing the patient from family home into a residential rehabilitation program for 12 months
options.rationale: Separation is not standard of care and disrupts a supportive attachment; structured family work addresses the specific expressed emotion pattern without separation (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

explanation.summary: Structured family intervention (family psychoeducation, communication skills, problem solving, and modification of high expressed emotion) delivered over at least 3 months by trained clinicians reduces relapse in first episode psychosis by about 50 percent at 12 months. High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement) is the single most robust family predictor of relapse. Interventions include the patient wherever possible and combine group and individual family sessions. Single session psychoeducation, peer support, and separation from family are less effective when used alone. This intervention sits alongside medication adherence work, vocational recovery, and physical health monitoring.
key_points: Structured family intervention over 3 or more months
High expressed emotion is a major relapse predictor
Reduces relapse by around 50 percent at 12 months
explanation.pearls: Reducing criticism and emotional overinvolvement is more effective than raising warmth alone; simple weekly problem solving meetings taught to families can achieve this over 8 to 12 sessions.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition on prednisolone taper
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man who was tapered off prednisolone 4 weeks ago after 18 months of 15 to 20 mg daily for pemphigus vulgaris. He was reduced from 5 mg every second day to zero over 3 weeks. He is now on day 4 of an upper respiratory tract infection with fevers to 38.6 and rigors. Today he attended the emergency department after collapsing at home when he stood up quickly.

Examination: he is drowsy but rousable, mucosal pallor, deeply tanned in sun exposed areas. Vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg (unresponsive to a 500 mL saline bolus already given), respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest x-ray shows early right lower zone consolidation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 76/44 (unresponsive to 500 mL saline), RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, temp 38.9
data_table.Steroid history: Prednisolone 15 to 20 mg daily x 18 months, tapered off 4 weeks ago
data_table.Bloods: Na 128; K+ 5.4; glucose 3.1 mmol/L; urea 12.4; creatinine 148
data_table.Skin: Deeply tanned in sun exposed areas; mucosal pallor

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and doxycycline 100 mg for community acquired pneumonia as primary treatment
options.rationale: Antibiotics are appropriate for the pneumonia, but they do not address the underlying adrenal crisis that is producing the refractory hypotension; hydrocortisone must be given first (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion titrated to mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg via central line access
options.rationale: Vasopressors will fail without cortisol replacement in adrenal crisis; noradrenaline is not a substitute for hydrocortisone here (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent sodium chloride 100 mL bolus to correct hyponatraemia before other interventions
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is secondary to cortisol deficiency and corrects with hydrocortisone plus isotonic saline; hypertonic saline is not indicated without neurological symptoms (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Send a short synacthen test now and defer any glucocorticoid until baseline and 30 minute cortisol return
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis and any diagnostic delay is dangerous; hydrocortisone should be given immediately and a stimulation test performed later, or a random cortisol drawn just before dosing (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with concurrent normal saline resuscitation and glucose
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical emergency; intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours) with isotonic saline and glucose correction is the primary treatment; delay for testing worsens outcomes (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in a patient recently withdrawn from long term supraphysiological glucocorticoid therapy is a clinical diagnosis: hypotension unresponsive to fluid, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and precipitating stressor (here, sepsis and pneumonia). Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours as continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, plus isotonic saline resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia are the immediate mainstay. Treatment must not wait for cortisol testing (a random pre-treatment cortisol can be drawn if easily done). Antibiotics for the precipitant follow. Once stable, transition to oral hydrocortisone with a written sick day plan, medic alert bracelet, and self-injection education.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours
Isotonic saline resuscitation and glucose correction concurrently
Do not delay treatment for the short synacthen test
explanation.pearls: Any patient on more than 5 mg prednisolone equivalent daily for more than 3 weeks has HPA axis suppression risk; sick day rules and a hydrocortisone emergency kit prevent crisis.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia intravenous iron choice
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45 year old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids. She has 6 months of fatigue and shortness of breath climbing stairs. She has trialled two oral iron products (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and iron polymaltose 100 mg elemental daily) but stopped both within 2 weeks because of intolerable epigastric pain and constipation. She is on the waitlist for a Mirena insertion in 8 weeks.

Bloods: haemoglobin 82 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 74 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 4 micrograms/L (30 to 200), transferrin saturation 6 percent (16 to 45), CRP 3 mg/L (less than 5). Coeliac serology and faecal occult blood are negative. She has no history of severe allergy or asthma, is not pregnant, and is otherwise well. She weighs 68 kg, and her calculated iron deficit (Ganzoni formula) is approximately 1200 mg.

data_table.Iron studies: Hb 82; MCV 74; ferritin 4; transferrin saturation 6 percent
data_table.Oral iron trial: Ferrous sulfate and iron polymaltose both stopped within 2 weeks for GI intolerance
data_table.Cause of loss: Heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids; Mirena in 8 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for iron replacement?

options.text: Single dose intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes with 15 minutes post infusion monitoring
options.rationale: Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV over at least 15 minutes with 30 minutes post infusion monitoring is standard for oral iron intolerance in the PBS-listed indication of iron deficiency anaemia; a single dose covers a deficit up to 1000 mg (Source: PBS Ferric Carboxymaltose Listing).

options.text: Restart oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with a proton pump inhibitor 40 mg to reduce epigastric pain
options.rationale: PPI reduces gastric acid and impairs iron absorption; it is not a fix for oral iron intolerance and does not address her existing anaemia in a timely way (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells now to correct haemoglobin above 100 g/L rapidly
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia not manageable by iron replacement or with haemoglobin below 70 g/L (or 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease); this patient warrants iron replacement first (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Prescribe intramuscular iron dextran 100 mg alternate days for 12 weeks in the general practice setting
options.rationale: IM iron dextran is largely superseded by IV iron polymaltose or ferric carboxymaltose which are faster, better tolerated, and safer; IM dosing carries staining and slower correction (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Delay all iron replacement until the Mirena insertion in 8 weeks resolves the ongoing menstrual loss
options.rationale: Waiting 8 weeks in a symptomatic patient with haemoglobin 82 and severe iron deficiency is unsafe; correction is done in parallel with definitive management of the cause (Source: RACGP Iron Deficiency Position).

explanation.summary: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose has largely replaced iron polymaltose in Australia for oral iron intolerance and rapid correction. A single 1000 mg dose given over at least 15 minutes with 30 minutes of monitoring afterwards suffices for a deficit up to 1000 mg; larger deficits are made up 1 week later. Hypersensitivity is rare but staff must be trained in anaphylaxis management and pre-treatment history must screen for prior hypersensitivity reactions and severe atopy. Watch for hypophosphataemia after high dose FCM (check phosphate at 2 to 4 weeks if repeat dosing planned). Definitive management of the cause (Mirena for menorrhagia, endoscopy in men or postmenopausal women) proceeds in parallel.
key_points: Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV single dose over at least 15 minutes
Repeat 1 week later if deficit exceeds 1000 mg
Manage the cause in parallel; do not delay for definitive treatment
explanation.pearls: Extravasation of ferric carboxymaltose causes long lasting brown skin staining; large bore cannula in a straight vein above the wrist minimises this risk.

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman for assessment of what she wonders is autism. She reports lifelong difficulty in social groups (she can manage one to one but finds groups exhausting), intense special interests (marine biology since age 6, currently a competitive knitter with detailed knowledge of yarn weights), a need for predictable routines (rings her sister the same time every Thursday), and sensory overload in supermarkets that she manages with noise cancelling headphones.

She scored 32 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10 not shown), scored 42 on the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale Revised, and describes exhaustion after long social days that she calls masking. Her school reports describe her as a well behaved bright student who kept to herself. She has no learning disability. Screening scores: PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 8. She uses no alcohol or illicit substances. She has never had a psychiatric diagnosis previously.

data_table.Core features: Social exhaustion; special interests; routines; sensory overload
data_table.Development: School reports describe reserved bright student

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step to make a confident DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: Prescribe an SSRI first line for probable social anxiety disorder and reassess autism features in 6 months
options.rationale: Attributing the presentation to social anxiety without full assessment risks missing autism spectrum disorder; the pattern here (early onset, special interests, sensory, routines) is not social anxiety (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

options.text: Advise she does not meet DSM-5 criteria because her school reports describe a well behaved child without concern
options.rationale: Autistic girls and women commonly present as well behaved in school reports because of masking; absence of behavioural concerns in childhood does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position).
source_refs: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position

options.text: Order genetic testing (chromosomal microarray) as the primary confirmatory diagnostic test in a well adult
options.rationale: Genetic testing is offered in children where a specific syndrome is suspected; in adults without intellectual disability it is not the diagnostic step (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

options.text: Refer for structured multidisciplinary assessment using DSM-5 criteria including collateral developmental history
options.rationale: NICE CG142 and Australian autism diagnostic guidelines recommend structured multidisciplinary assessment including a developmental history from a knowledgeable informant, DSM-5 criteria review, and validated tools such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule or interview (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

options.text: Prescribe methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily as a therapeutic trial for likely ADHD comorbidity
options.rationale: A stimulant trial is not a diagnostic test for autism spectrum disorder and would not clarify the presenting picture; formal ADHD assessment is separate and does not substitute (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

explanation.summary: Adult autism spectrum disorder in women is under recognised because of masking (learned social scripts, mimicking peers, camouflage). Presentation includes lifelong social exhaustion, restricted interests (often narrower topic focus that can be socially acceptable), routines, and sensory sensitivities. DSM-5 requires persistent deficits in social communication and interaction (across multiple settings), restricted or repetitive behaviours (at least two), symptoms present in early childhood (though masked), clinically significant impairment, and no better explanation. Diagnosis rests on structured multidisciplinary assessment including a developmental history from a knowledgeable informant (parent, older sibling, longstanding friend), review of school and childhood records, and use of validated tools (ADOS-2, ADI-R, DISCO). Screening tools like AQ and RAADS-R suggest but do not confirm the diagnosis.
key_points: Masking commonly hides autism in women and girls
DSM-5 requires early onset even if only apparent in retrospect
Diagnosis by structured multidisciplinary assessment with informant
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about school playground time (spent alone or with a single peer, watching from the edge, playing structured games only); adult recall of primary school playtime is often more diagnostic than academic performance.

subtopic_detail: Conversion vs factitious vs malingering discrimination
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34 year old primary school teacher admitted 4 days ago with right sided leg weakness that began abruptly after she witnessed a serious playground injury. She describes the leg as heavy and unable to move, is unable to weight bear, and slides the leg rather than lifting it. There is no bowel or bladder involvement. She is not seeking any financial gain and returned to work is her goal.

On examination: power in the right lower limb 0 out of 5 for hip flexion and knee extension when directly tested, but she is observed to move the same leg to reposition herself in bed. Hoover sign is positive (left hip extension is weak on request but strong when asked to flex the right hip against resistance). Reflexes are symmetric and normal, plantar responses are downgoing. MRI brain and whole spine, nerve conduction studies, and creatine kinase are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of malingering, factitious disorder, or Munchausen syndrome.

data_table.Neurology: Right leg 0/5 direct; observed spontaneous movement; Hoover positive
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and whole spine normal; NCS and CK normal
data_table.Onset: Abruptly after witnessing serious playground injury
data_table.Motivation: Return to work; no external incentive; no factitious history

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Malingering, discharge with letter to insurance, no further specialist input needed given no genuine impairment
options.rationale: Malingering requires external incentive (compensation, avoiding duty, obtaining medication) which is absent here; her goal is return to work; symptoms are not consciously produced (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self, admission for behavioural observation to catch deliberate feigning
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires intentional falsification of symptoms motivated by adopting the sick role; there is no evidence of intentional falsification and she is not seeking the sick role (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Functional neurological (conversion) disorder, referral for physiotherapy and psychology with clear diagnostic explanation
options.rationale: DSM-5 functional neurological (conversion) disorder requires positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign, spontaneous movement out of keeping with formal testing); management is delivering a clear positive diagnosis, physiotherapy, and psychological therapy, not repeat imaging (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder, commence duloxetine 60 mg daily for chronic pain and refer to pain clinic
options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder focuses on excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours about somatic symptoms; conversion disorder is a distinct diagnosis with positive neurological signs of incongruity (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Repeat MRI brain and whole spine with gadolinium plus lumbar puncture to exclude occult demyelinating disease
options.rationale: Repeat neuroimaging without new clinical features reinforces illness behaviour and undermines the positive diagnosis; conversion disorder requires positive signs, not exclusion (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 renamed conversion disorder as functional neurological symptom disorder to emphasise that the diagnosis rests on positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment, tubular visual fields) rather than an exclusion diagnosis. Management is delivering a clear positive explanation using neutral, non stigmatising language, engaging the patient in physiotherapy with a graded rehabilitation approach, and psychological therapy for common comorbid anxiety or trauma. Repeated imaging and specialist referrals reinforce illness behaviour and worsen outcome. Malingering (intentional falsification for external gain) and factitious disorder (intentional falsification to adopt the sick role) are separate diagnoses; both require intentional deception which is absent in conversion disorder.
key_points: Positive signs (Hoover, entrainment) confirm the diagnosis
Deliver a clear positive explanation early to aid recovery
Physiotherapy plus psychology; avoid repeat imaging
explanation.pearls: Websites like neurosymptoms.org (Jon Stone) are useful patient information adjuncts; sharing the positive diagnostic reasoning with the patient improves prognosis more than months of exclusion investigations.

stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with progressive breathlessness on exertion over 8 weeks and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a 40 pack year smoking history, quit 2 years ago. On examination he has stony dull percussion and reduced breath sounds over the left lower zone. Chest x-ray shows a moderate left pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound guided pleurocentesis is performed and 40 mL of straw coloured pleural fluid is aspirated.

Pleural fluid analysis: protein 38 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 320 U/L, glucose 4.1 mmol/L, pH 7.36. Serum protein 62 g/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase 210 U/L (upper limit of normal 240 U/L). Cytology and culture are pending. Bloods: full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, NT-proBNP 82 ng/L (less than 125). Echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function.

data_table.Imaging: Moderate left pleural effusion on CXR

lead_in: How should the pleural fluid be classified using Light's criteria and what is the next step?

options.text: Transudate; initiate loop diuretic therapy and repeat chest x-ray in 2 weeks without further evaluation
options.rationale: Fluid protein 38 g/L (ratio 0.61, above 0.5) meets Light's criteria for an exudate, not a transudate; loop diuretic without cause is inappropriate (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Exudate; arrange contrast enhanced CT chest and consider pleural biopsy given smoking history and unilateral effusion
options.rationale: Pleural protein to serum protein ratio 0.61 (above 0.5) and pleural LDH to serum LDH ratio 1.52 (above 0.6) meet 2 of 3 Light's criteria for exudate; contrast CT and pleural biopsy are indicated to exclude malignancy given age, smoking history, and unilateral effusion (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Exudate; initiate empirical broad spectrum antibiotics and arrange chest drain insertion for empyema treatment
options.rationale: The fluid has pH 7.36 and glucose 4.1 mmol/L with no purulence, which does not meet criteria for empyema; empirical antibiotics and drain are not indicated without those features (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Transudate; commence NT-proBNP based heart failure workup and add angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor immediately
options.rationale: NT-proBNP is normal and echocardiogram normal; the fluid meets exudate criteria not transudate; heart failure is not the cause (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Indeterminate; repeat pleurocentesis in 4 weeks with albumin gradient to establish the effusion aetiology later
options.rationale: The Light's criteria are met for exudate; workup should proceed now with CT and biopsy rather than await repeat tap (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

explanation.summary: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as exudate if any one of pleural to serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural to serum LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH is met. This patient's protein ratio is 0.61 and LDH ratio 1.52 (both criteria met). Common exudative causes are malignancy, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, and connective tissue disease. Unilateral exudative effusion in a smoker over 50 warrants contrast CT chest and image guided pleural biopsy (or medical thoracoscopy) to exclude malignancy including mesothelioma. Fluid pH below 7.2, glucose below 3.3 mmol/L, or frank pus indicate complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema and require chest drain.
key_points: Light's criteria (any 1 of 3) define exudate
Unilateral exudate in a smoker over 50: CT chest and biopsy
Fluid pH below 7.2 or glucose below 3.3 mmol/L: drain empyema
explanation.pearls: If diuretic therapy has been given before the tap, the pleural to serum albumin gradient (above 12 g/L implies transudate) is more reliable than Light's criteria, which can falsely classify diuretic-treated transudates as exudates.
